title: I recently watched Dazed and Confused. I have a couple of questions.

commenti.body:
I think that is a lot of the point with Dazed and Confused - it doesn’t tell a narrative story as much as it captures a specific, time, place, and feeling (coming of age in Austin, TX in the 70’s, but relatable to a lot of other folks with different experiences).

Doesn’t mean it has to be your cup of tea! But what I got out of it.

Dazed and Confused can be situated within a number of one-night-where-everything-happens coming of age stories. American Graffiti is the progenitor of this basic setup as I understand it. Superbad is another example even if it’s significantly goofier and more outlandish. Booksmart is a more recent example. 

Dazed and Confused really does feel like Richard Linklater was making a version of American Graffiti for his generation, so it’s more dialogue-heavy and has many overlapping storylines unlike the recent examples I mentioned.

I would also consider Kicking and Screaming (1995) in the same vein though it takes place over a longer span of time. The basic vibe is: School is ending and it’s time to get out into the real world and grapple with all that comes with that step in life. 

Personally, I have aged out of enjoying these kinds of stories as they are about a time in life that is well behind me. But I was fond of them when I was younger.

"In other words, the filmmaker did not feel the need to have scenes where we are introduced to characters and their conflicts and them overcoming them"

  
He did though. It's just that those conflicts are internal and emotional, and more *story* dependent than *plot* dependent. Pink is torn between the straight path and the winding one. Kevin is torn between youth and young adulthood. Cynthia, Tony, and Mike are torn between acceptance and withdrawal. 

Character is revealed through story, and less through plot, and Linklater is concerned more with feeling, tone, and realism than bombastic stakes. It's a hangout movie. A snapshot. Linklater wants you to get lost, to feel like there are additional threads just waiting to be pulled. In a lesser film, the goofball Kevin is likely the main character. It is true to life, and it makes the characters feel lived in over just archetypes.

This may not be your type of movie, but I consider it a masterpiece, and a lovely companion to his later (and similar) film Everybody Wants Some!!! But regardless of the viewer's taste, I think Linklater achieved his creative goals and that is worthy of admiration.

This movie takes place in the late 70s. I think I was around 9 or 10 years old at the time. This movie is really about capturing the spirit of the times. I remember my  friends older siblings being like many of the characters.  The clothes, music, and slang, and what took place at school and on the weekends.  While I didn't connect with or identify with any one character, I connected with the film as a whole. It's pretty spot-on.

Yep.  You're describing Linklater's style.  It's intentional and doesn't resonate with everyone.  Lots of essays written about him and his style and especially *Slacker* as a debut.  Here's one that goes into some description about how the structure and cuts (or lack of them) feed the feelings you're describing: https://www.sensesofcinema.com/2003/great-directors/linklater/.

I'm pretty old too, but I think the movies like Dazed & Confused are important for showing people that the period was not as sanitized as most media portrayed it, and thereby undercutting the lie that the present day is the most permissive and progressive in history.

I'm curious how many other Richard Linklater films you've seen, and which ones. He obviously has more traditional stuff like School of Rock, but a lot of his films largely consist of characters just talking to each other in a naturalistic way. He was a huge influence on Kevin Smith and his film Slacker was the direct inspiration for Clerks, which is also mostly just two people talking to each other.

I love the film because for its nostalgic slice-of-life portrayal of the end of high school, how authentic it feels while still having interpersonal drama. I actually think the characters are really strong and easily identifiable, not just in what they say but how they present themselves. I didn't need to be told that Rory Cochrane's character was a stoner because he looks and acts like one.
Yes. The OP really made me think of *Slacker*.
*SubUrbia* is another example of a Linklater film much more about characters talking to each other than about plot.

>Did anybody else feel like they were watching a documentary than a fictional movie? As if the filmmaker just had a bunch of cameras in different places and recorded whatever is happening? In other words, the filmmaker did not feel the need to have scenes where we are introduced to characters and their conflicts and them overcoming them, in a way that other fictional movies typically do? If so, how did the filmmaker accomplish this? I think that might partly explain why I wasn't able to connect with the characters.

Do you enjoy other movies or novels that fall under this 'slice of life' category? Say, *Clerks* or the short stories of Raymond Carver or Linklater's debut film *Slacker* or early Satyajit Ray or Abbas Kiarostami films? 

It's an aesthetic experience that many writers and filmmakers and artists have gone after: the experience of just watching something like real life unfold, without the heightened drama or narrative patterns of typical stories.

As you say, it's really a matter of taste. Some people really resonate with media like this and some do not.
I've not seen that one, it looks even more like Clerks! I love Richard Linklater but there's so many I haven't seen because he's got about a billion movies.
